## 4. lore — Lore: the mouth that is also a door, and the to-me that feelings arrive at

**ANNA:** Lore: the mouth that is also a door, and the to-me that feelings arrive at

**ANNA:** வாய்
> This is vaai. Mouth. But a mouth is an opening, and Tamil never forgets that.

**ANNA:** வாயில்
> Put it in the locative and you get vaayil, which is 'in the mouth'. It is also the word for a doorway. A door is just a mouth in a wall.

**ANNA:** வாய் திறந்தா காக்கா கொத்திட்டு போயிடும்
> That is why the crow line works. Open your mouth and the crow will peck at it and carry something off. It is what you say to someone standing there gaping, because an open mouth is an open door and anything can walk in.

**ANNA:** பரவாயில்லை
> Here is a trick of sound. Paravaayillai ends in what looks like 'vaai illai', no mouth. It isn't. That is a coincidence. The word most likely comes from a Persian and Hindi word for concern, so it means 'no concern'.

**ANNA:** எனக்கு
> Now enakku. Two pieces: en, which is 'my', and kku, which is 'to' or 'for'. So it is literally 'to my'.

**ANNA:** The plain word for I, naan, never takes an ending. Before any case ending it steps aside and en takes its place. That is why you never hear naan with a kku on it.

**ANNA:** A textbook glosses enakku as 'I', and that misses it. Tamil does not say I like idli. It says to me, idli is pleasing. Liking, knowing, being in a hurry, they all arrive at you. You are where they land.

**ANNA:** எனக்கு புரியல
> So this is 'to me, it isn't understood'. Not 'I don't understand'. Nobody is failing. It just didn't arrive.
